fuentes/codice-de-dresde/soporte.texto: Accordion-folded book of stuccoed bark paper (amate), 39 leaves painted on both sides; Saxon State and University Library, Dresden

fuentes/codice-de-dresde/resumen.texto: The most complete and best preserved of the four surviving pre-Hispanic Maya books. It contains 260-day divinatory almanacs, tables of the cycles of Venus and of eclipses, New Year rituals, and a final scene of a flood. Johann Christian Götze bought it in Vienna in 1739 for the Royal Library of Dresden. It got wet in the bombing of 1945, and some pages were damaged.

fuentes/codice-de-dresde/por_que_importa.texto: It is the basis of knowledge of Maya astronomy and the calendar: in the 19th century Förstemann used it to explain the Long Count and the Venus tables, and in 1952 Knorozov used it to test syllabic reading. It is believed to be a copy of an earlier original.

fuentes/codice-de-dresde/leer.0.titulo.texto: Complete digital facsimile from the Saxon State and University Library (Dresden)

fuentes/codice-de-dresde/leer.1.titulo.texto: Reproductions of the codex at FAMSI

fuentes/codice-de-madrid/soporte.texto: Folding screen of coated amate paper, 112 pages; Museo de América, Madrid

fuentes/codice-de-madrid/resumen.texto: The longest of the Maya codices, with 260-day almanacs for planting, hunting, beekeeping, rain and crafts, and scenes of gods, among them scenes of sacrifice. It appeared in Spain in two parts, the Troano and the Cortesiano, which León de Rosny recognized in 1880 as a single book. Its date is disputed: most place it in the Late Postclassic period.

fuentes/codice-de-madrid/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the practical religion of Postclassic Yucatán and the calendar used for each task of the year, and it was one of the texts used to test the decipherment.

fuentes/codice-de-madrid/leer.0.titulo.texto: Reproductions of the codex at FAMSI

fuentes/codice-de-paris/soporte.texto: Fragment of 11 amate leaves painted on both sides; National Library of France

fuentes/codice-de-paris/resumen.texto: Fragment of a Maya book with prophecies for a series of katuns (periods of about twenty years) and their patron gods, an almanac of constellations, and ceremonies at the end of periods. León de Rosny found it in 1859 in the Imperial Library in Paris, very worn at the edges.

fuentes/codice-de-paris/por_que_importa.texto: Its katun prophecies have parallels in the Books of Chilam Balam, written centuries later in the Latin alphabet, which shows the continuity of that tradition under Spanish rule.

fuentes/codice-de-paris/leer.0.titulo.texto: Reproductions of the codex at FAMSI

fuentes/codice-maya-de-mexico/titulo.texto: Maya Codex of Mexico (formerly the Grolier Codex)

fuentes/codice-maya-de-mexico/soporte.texto: Ten fragmentary pages of a screen of amate of about twenty; National Museum of Anthropology, Mexico

fuentes/codice-maya-de-mexico/resumen.texto: Almanac of the cycles of Venus, of which ten pages survive, with figures of armed gods and captives. It appeared in the 1960s in the hands of a Mexican collector, probably looted from a cave in Chiapas, and was exhibited at the Grolier Club in New York in 1971. Thompson and others considered it a forgery. A study by Coe, Houston, Miller and Taube (2016) and analyses by the INAH (2018) dated it between 1021 and 1154 and declared it authentic.

fuentes/codice-maya-de-mexico/por_que_im.texto: According to the INAH, it is the oldest book from America that survives; it is also the only Maya codex on the continent. Its case shows how archaeological looting destroys information about the origin of pieces.

fuentes/codice-maya-de-mexico/leer.0.tit.texto: Photographs of the codex at FAMSI

fuentes/codice-zouche-nuttall/soporte.texto: Deerskin screen of 47 leaves; British Museum, London

fuentes/codice-zouche-nuttall/resumen.texto: Painted Mixtec book with genealogies and deeds of the lordships of the Mixteca. One side narrates the history of Tilantongo and Teozacoalco, and the other the life of Eight Deer Jaguar Claw, with his conquests, marriage alliances and sacrifices of captives. In the 19th century it was held in a convent in Florence; its name comes from its owner, Baron Zouche, and from Zelia Nuttall, who published it in 1902.

fuentes/codice-zouche-nuttall/por_que_im.texto: Together with the Bodley, the Vindobonensis and the Colombino-Becker, it allows reconstruction of more than four centuries of Mixtec dynastic history, one of the few pre-Hispanic histories dated year by year.

fuentes/codice-vindobonense/soporte.texto: Deerskin screen of 52 leaves; Austrian National Library, Vienna

fuentes/codice-vindobonense/resumen.texto: Mixtec codex with the origin of the world and of the Mixtec lineages according to their tradition, with the hero Nine Wind, and on the other side the genealogy of the lords of Tilantongo. It probably reached Europe among the objects sent by Cortés in 1519; it passed through Italy and in the 17th century reached the imperial library in Vienna.

fuentes/codice-vindobonense/por_que_impo.texto: It is the main source on Mixtec cosmogony and one of the few books known to have been sent to Europe before the fall of Tenochtitlan.

fuentes/codice-bodley/resumen.texto: Mixtec genealogical codex with the history of the dynasties of Tilantongo and other lordships, including the career of Eight Deer, up to the eve of the Spanish conquest. It has been in the Bodleian Library in Oxford since the early 17th century.

fuentes/codice-bodley/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the latest Mixtec codices, and it links the history of Eight Deer with the lineages that governed the Mixteca when the Spaniards arrived.

fuentes/codice-colombino/soporte.texto: Deerskin screen; National Museum of Anthropology, Mexico (the Becker I fragment is in Vienna)

fuentes/codice-colombino/resumen.texto: Fragment of a Mixtec codex devoted to the life of Eight Deer, another part of which survives in Vienna (the Codex Becker I). In the 16th century parts of the painting were scraped off and glosses in Mixtec were added, because it was used as evidence in land disputes between towns.

fuentes/codice-colombino/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the most detailed accounts of the life of Eight Deer, and an example of how Indigenous peoples used their ancient books in colonial courts.

fuentes/codice-borgia/soporte.texto: Deerskin screen of 39 leaves painted on both sides (76 pages); Vatican Apostolic Library

fuentes/codice-borgia/resumen.texto: Divinatory and ritual book from central Mexico, with the 260-day almanac, the gods who govern each period, and scenes of rites, among them human sacrifice and self-sacrifice. It belonged to Cardinal Stefano Borgia in the 18th century and gives its name to the Borgia group, the set of pre-Hispanic religious codices of that region.

fuentes/codice-borgia/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most important of the pre-Hispanic religious codices of central Mexico to survive the conquest. Without it, that religion would be known almost only from what the friars wrote.

fuentes/codice-borgia/leer.0.titulo.texto: Complete digital facsimile from the Vatican Apostolic Library

fuentes/libros-de-chilam-balam/soporte.texto: Manuscripts from several Yucatec towns (Chumayel, Tizimín, Maní, Kaua, Ixil and others), copied and recopied until the 19th century

fuentes/libros-de-chilam-balam/resumen.texto: Books written in Yucatec Maya in the Latin alphabet that bear the name of the priest Chilam Balam, to whom they attribute the prophecy of the arrival of foreigners. They mix katun prophecies, chronicles of the history of the Itzás, Chichén Itzá and Mayapán, calendars, medicine and translated Christian texts. The Chumayel book was copied in 1782 and the Tizimín book in the 18th century.

fuentes/libros-de-chilam-balam/por_que_i.texto: They are the written voice of the Yucatec Maya under Spanish rule, and they preserve, transformed, contents of the ancient hieroglyphic books. Their katun chronicles are hard to date and should be read with caution.

fuentes/libros-de-chilam-balam/leer.0.ti.texto: Photographic facsimile of the Chumayel manuscript published by the University of Pennsylvania Museum (1913), with an English introduction by G. B. Gordon, on the Internet Archive

fuentes/anales-de-los-cakchiqueles/titul.texto: Memorial de Sololá (Annals of the Kaqchikels)

fuentes/anales-de-los-cakchiqueles/autor.texto: Francisco Hernández Arana Xajilá and Francisco Rojas

fuentes/anales-de-los-cakchiqueles/sopor.texto: Manuscript found in 1844 in the archive of the convent of San Francisco in Guatemala, which Brasseur de Bourbourg translated in 1855; today at the University of Pennsylvania

fuentes/anales-de-los-cakchiqueles/resum.texto: Chronicle of the Xajil lineage of the Kaqchikels: their mythical origin in Tulán, the migrations, the wars with the K’iche’, the founding of Iximché and the arrival of Pedro de Alvarado in 1524. It recounts the epidemic that killed much of the population around 1520, before the Spaniards arrived in Guatemala, the initial alliance, the gold tribute demanded by Alvarado, the Kaqchikel rebellion and the forced labor that followed. It continues afterward as a record of deaths and events of the people until 1604.

fuentes/anales-de-los-cakchiqueles/por_q.texto: It is one of the few Indigenous chronicles of Mesoamerica that narrates the conquest year by year, and from the perspective of a people that was first an ally and then a rebel.

fuentes/anales-de-los-cakchiqueles/leer..texto: English translation by Daniel G. Brinton (1885), with the Kaqchikel text, on Project Gutenberg

fuentes/rabinal-achi/autor.texto: Achí oral tradition (transcribed by Bartolo Sis)

fuentes/rabinal-achi/soporte.texto: Danced drama; Bartolo Sis wrote the text down in 1850, and Brasseur de Bourbourg published it in 1862

fuentes/rabinal-achi/resumen.texto: Danced drama of the Achí of Rabinal about the capture of the K’iche’ warrior Achí by the men of Rabinal, his trial before the lord Job’Toj, and his death by sacrifice. The dialogue recounts the wars, abductions and tributes between the two lordships. It is still performed in Rabinal every January.

fuentes/rabinal-achi/por_que_importa.texto: It is considered the only surviving Mesoamerican drama of pre-Hispanic origin, showing war and the sacrifice of captives from within. UNESCO proclaimed it a masterpiece of the oral heritage in 2005.

fuentes/rabinal-achi/leer.0.titulo.texto: First edition, with the Achí text and Brasseur de Bourbourg’s French translation (1862), on the Internet Archive

fuentes/titulo-de-totonicapan/soporte.texto: Manuscript signed by K’iche’ lords in 1554; Spanish translation of 1834; the original reappeared in 1973

fuentes/titulo-de-totonicapan/resumen.texto: K’iche’ document that narrates the origin, migrations and conquests of the lineages of Q’umarkaj, with accounts similar to those of the Popol Vuh. Indigenous lords wrote it to prove their rights before the Spanish authorities.

fuentes/titulo-de-totonicapan/por_que_im.texto: It confirms and completes the history of the K’iche’ kingdoms in the Popol Vuh, and it shows how the land titles of Indigenous communities preserved pre-Hispanic memory.

fuentes/relacion-de-michoacan/soporte.texto: Manuscript with 44 paintings by Indigenous artists; Royal Library of San Lorenzo de El Escorial

fuentes/relacion-de-michoacan/resumen.texto: Account written for Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza with the narratives of elders and priests of the Purépecha. It tells the story of Tariácuri and his heirs, the wars of conquest of the kingdom, war as a religious duty to bring firewood and captives to the god Curicaueri, the sacrifice of prisoners, the justice of the cazonci, and the arrival of the Spaniards up to the execution of the last king, Tangáxuan II, by Nuño de Guzmán in 1530. Of the first part, on the gods and the festivals, only a single folio survives.

fuentes/relacion-de-michoacan/por_que_im.texto: It is almost the only source on the Purépecha kingdom, the great rival of the Mexica, and one of the few early chronicles that tell the conquest from the perspective of the defeated.

fuentes/relacion-de-michoacan/leer.0.tit.texto: Mexican edition of 1903, on the Internet Archive

fuentes/relacion-de-las-cosas-de-yucatan.texto: Relación de las cosas de Yucatán
The original was lost; an abbreviated 17th-century copy survives in the Royal Academy of History in Madrid, which Brasseur de Bourbourg found and published in 1864

Description of Yucatán and of the Maya written by Landa in Spain while he defended himself against the charges arising from the 1562 trials. It tells the history of Chichén Itzá and Mayapán, the Spanish conquest, the calendar, festivals, slavery, war and human sacrifice, including the sacrifices in the cenote of Chichén Itzá, the flaying of victims and the sharing out of their flesh. It includes the so-called Maya alphabet. It acknowledges that the friars burned the Maya books they found because they considered them the work of the devil, and it records cruelties by the conquistadors in Cupul, Yobaín, Cochuah and Chetumal (lords burned alive, women hanged with their children from a tree he says he saw, mutilations), which in his account reduced the population.

It is the main written source on the Maya of the conquest period, and the key that allowed the calendars to be deciphered and, from 1952, syllabic writing. It was written by the same man who directed the repression at Maní, and its text justifies that campaign.
Edition by Brasseur de Bourbourg (Paris, 1864), Spanish text with French translation, on Project Gutenberg

fuentes/procesos-de-idolatria-de-yucatan.texto: Trials and inquiries into idolatry in Yucatán (1562–1565)
Diego Quijada, Diego de Landa, Francisco de Toral and others (ed. France V. Scholes and Eleanor B. Adams, 1938)
Files from the General Archive of the Indies, published in Mexico in 1938

Testimony, interrogations, letters and inquiries from the idolatry trials that Landa and the chief magistrate Diego Quijada conducted in Maní, Sotuta and Hocabá in 1562, and from the later investigation by Bishop Toral and the complaints of encomenderos and Maya lords. They record the use of torture (hanging with weights and whipping), the deaths and suicides of detainees, and confessions of human sacrifice, some within churches. Their credibility is debated because they were obtained under torture.
They are the direct documentation of the auto de fe of Maní, and they allow Landa’s version to be checked against that of his critics. Inga Clendinnen analyzed them in Ambivalent Conquests (1987).

fuentes/bloque-de-cascajal/soporte.texto: Serpentine block of about 36 by 21 centimeters with 62 incised signs

fuentes/bloque-de-cascajal/resumen.texto: Stone block with 62 signs in rows, which workers found in 1999 among the material of a quarry near San Lorenzo, Veracruz. A Mexican and American team published it in Science in 2006 as the oldest text in America, dated to around 900 BC by the pottery associated with it.

fuentes/bloque-de-cascajal/por_que_impor.texto: If it is writing, it pushes back by several centuries the origin of Mesoamerican writing systems. Because it was not found in an excavation, some critics doubted its authenticity or date, and it is debated whether the signs form a text: there is no other similar example.

fuentes/monumento-3-de-san-jose-mogote/s.texto: Stone slab placed as a threshold between two public buildings

fuentes/monumento-3-de-san-jose-mogote/r.texto: Carved slab showing a naked man lying down, with scrolls of blood coming from his chest, and a calendar glyph, “1 Earthquake,” which would be his name. Kent Flannery and Joyce Marcus interpret it as the depiction of a sacrificed captive, placed so that it would be trodden on when passing.

fuentes/monumento-3-de-san-jose-mogote/p.texto: For its excavators it is the oldest example of Zapotec writing and of the association between writing, calendar and the sacrifice of enemies in Oaxaca. Other researchers propose a later date.

fuentes/danzantes-de-monte-alban/soporte.texto: More than 300 carved slabs, most in the gallery of Building L at Monte Albán

fuentes/danzantes-de-monte-alban/resumen.texto: Slabs with figures of naked men in twisted postures, with eyes closed and, in some cases, genitals mutilated and bleeding, sometimes accompanied by glyphs. The first descriptions took them to be dancers. The interpretation most accepted today, by Joyce Marcus and others, is that they depict dead or sacrificed enemies displayed in the center of the new capital.

fuentes/danzantes-de-monte-alban/por_que.texto: They are the largest set of images of war and sacrifice from the Mesoamerican Preclassic, and one of the earliest examples of writing in Oaxaca.

fuentes/estela-1-de-la-mojarra/soporte.texto: Basalt stela of about four tons, found in 1986 in the Acula River; Museum of Anthropology in Xalapa

fuentes/estela-1-de-la-mojarra/resumen.texto: Stela with a richly dressed ruler and a text of about 500 signs in Isthmian writing, with two Long Count dates corresponding to the years 143 and 156. John Justeson and Terrence Kaufman proposed in 1993 a decipherment that speaks of enthronement and war. Stephen Houston and Michael Coe tested it in 2003 with another text and concluded that it did not work.

fuentes/estela-1-de-la-mojarra/por_que_i.texto: It is the longest text in Isthmian writing, which is related to the Olmec tradition, and it shows that the Long Count was used outside the Maya area.

fuentes/murales-de-san-bartolo/soporte.texto: Fresco paintings in the Las Pinturas building at San Bartolo, Petén

fuentes/murales-de-san-bartolo/resumen.texto: Murals that William Saturno found in 2001 inside a pyramid. They narrate the myth of the maize god, the creation of the world and the enthronement of a king, with hieroglyphic texts. In 2006 Saturno, David Stuart and Boris Beltrán published in Science a text painted on an earlier layer of the same building, dated by radiocarbon to between 300 and 200 BC.

fuentes/murales-de-san-bartolo/por_que_i.texto: They show that the writing, mythology and sacred kingship of the Classic Maya already existed fully centuries earlier, in the Preclassic.

fuentes/estela-31-de-tikal/soporte.texto: Limestone stela; found in 1960 by the University of Pennsylvania Museum project, buried inside a later temple

fuentes/estela-31-de-tikal/resumen.texto: Stela dedicated in 445 by King Siyaj Chan K’awiil II, depicted on the front with the regalia of Maya kingship and flanked by his father, Yax Nuun Ahiin I, dressed as a Teotihuacan warrior. The text on the back records the arrival of Siyaj K’ak’ in 378, on the same day that King Chak Tok Ich’aak I died, and the enthronement of Yax Nuun Ahiin, son of Spear-Thrower Owl.

fuentes/estela-31-de-tikal/por_que_impor.texto: It is the longest text of the Early Classic and the main source for the “entry” of 378 and for the relationship between Teotihuacan and the Maya, a topic on which specialists debate whether there was conquest, alliance or dynastic interference.

fuentes/escalinata-jeroglifica-2-de-dos-.texto: Steps carved in front of a building at Dos Pilas

Inscription commissioned by B'alaj Chan K'awiil that recounts his war with Tikal: his defeats and flights, the intervention of Calakmul on his behalf, and his victory in 679 over Nuun Ujol Chaak, with an image of captives lying beneath the victor’s feet.
It is the most detailed Maya account of a war between branches of the same dynasty, and it proves Dos Pilas’s alliance with Calakmul against Tikal.

fuentes/tableros-del-templo-de-las-inscr.texto: Panels of the Temple of the Inscriptions at Palenque
Scribes of K'inich Kan B'alam II
Three stone panels with 617 glyphs in the upper temple; sarcophagus lid of Pakal in the crypt

Texts completed by K'inich Kan B'alam II after the death of his father, Pakal, which review the history of the kings of Palenque and the end-of-katun ceremonies, including the attacks by Calakmul in 599 and 611. The sarcophagus lid, found in 1952, shows Pakal at the moment of his death, in the jaws of the underworld and beneath the world tree, with his name, dates and ancestors.
It is the second-longest known Maya inscription. Erich von Däniken used the lid in 1968 as supposed proof of an ancient astronaut; the texts of the tomb itself identify the figure and his death.

fuentes/altar-q-de-copan/autor.texto: Scribes of Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat

fuentes/altar-q-de-copan/soporte.texto: Stone block carved on four sides, in front of Temple 16

fuentes/altar-q-de-copan/resumen.texto: Altar commissioned in 776 by the sixteenth king of Copan, Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat. Its four sides show the sixteen rulers of the dynasty seated on their names, from the founder K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo', who hands the staff of office to Yax Pasaj; the text above narrates the founder’s arrival in 426-427.

fuentes/altar-q-de-copan/por_que_importa.texto: It summarizes the dynastic history of Copan on a single stone and was key to reconstructing the list of its kings.

fuentes/escalinata-jeroglifica-de-copan/.texto: Scribes of K'ak' Yipyaj Chan K'awiil
Stairway of 63 steps with about 2,200 glyphs on Temple 26

Stairway carved with the history of the Copan dynasty, dedicated in its final form in 755 by K'ak' Yipyaj Chan K'awiil, with statues of seated warrior kings on the steps. It is interpreted as an attempt to restore the dynasty’s prestige after the capture and sacrifice of Waxaklajuun Ub'aah K'awiil in 738. Much of it collapsed and was reassembled out of order in the 20th century.
It is the longest known Maya text, although the disorder of its blocks makes it impossible to read in full.

fuentes/dinteles-de-yaxchilan/soporte.texto: Three limestone lintels from Structure 23; Lintels 24 and 25 have been in the British Museum since Alfred Maudslay removed them in 1882, and Lintel 26 is in the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico

fuentes/dinteles-de-yaxchilan/resumen.texto: Lintels carved for the house of Lady K'ab'al Xook. Lintel 24 shows her drawing a cord with thorns through her tongue before her husband, Itzamnaaj B'alam III, who holds a torch, on a date of 709; Lintel 25 shows her before a vision serpent from whose mouth a warrior emerges; Lintel 26 shows her handing her husband his helmet before a battle.

fuentes/dinteles-de-yaxchilan/por_que_im.texto: They are the most precise images of blood autosacrifice by Maya nobility and of the ritual and political role of a court woman.

fuentes/murales-de-bonampak/idioma_origi.texto: Classic Maya (hieroglyphic texts in the scenes)

fuentes/murales-de-bonampak/soporte.texto: Frescoes in the three rooms of Structure 1 at Bonampak

fuentes/murales-de-bonampak/resumen.texto: Murals painted around 790 under King Yajaw Chan Muwaan. The first room shows the presentation of an heir and a procession with musicians; the second, a battle in the jungle and the presentation of naked captives whose fingernails have been torn out and who bleed from their fingers, next to a severed head; the third, dances and a ritual bloodletting by the royal family. They became known outside the region in 1946, when Lacandon guides led the photographer Giles Healey to them.

fuentes/murales-de-bonampak/por_que_impo.texto: They refuted the image of Classic Maya as a peaceful people ruled by astronomer priests, which Morley and Thompson had maintained, and they are the most complete representation of Maya warfare and of the treatment of captives.

fuentes/incidents-of-travel-in-central-a.texto: Incidents of Travel in Central America, Chiapas, and Yucatan
Two volumes with engravings by Frederick Catherwood

Account of Stephens and Catherwood’s journey through Central America during the civil war of the Federation, with the first detailed descriptions of Copan, Quirigua and Palenque. It recounts that Stephens bought the ruins of Copan for fifty dollars, and argues that these cities were built by the ancestors of the region’s Indigenous people, and not by peoples of the Old World.
It was a bestseller that made Maya civilization known in the United States and Europe and established the thesis of its American origin.

fuentes/incidents-of-travel-in-yucatan/s.texto: Two volumes with engravings by Frederick Catherwood

fuentes/incidents-of-travel-in-yucatan/r.texto: Account of Stephens and Catherwood’s second journey, through Yucatan, with descriptions of dozens of sites, among them Uxmal, Chichen Itza, Mayapan and Tulum. It discusses the texts of the Spanish chroniclers and concludes that some of these cities were inhabited when the Spaniards arrived.

fuentes/incidents-of-travel-in-yucatan/p.texto: It is the first systematic record of the ruins of northern Yucatan and one of the foundations of Maya archaeology.

fuentes/knorozov-1952/titulo.texto: The Ancient Writing of Central America

fuentes/knorozov-1952/soporte.texto: Article in the journal Sovetskaya Etnografiya (Moscow), issue 3 of 1952

fuentes/knorozov-1952/resumen.texto: Article in which Knorozov argued that Maya writing, like other ancient scripts, combined word signs with syllabic phonetic signs, and that Landa’s “alphabet” was in fact a list of syllables dictated by informants who misunderstood the question. With this method he proposed readings of words in the codices that were later confirmed. The journal included an ideological introduction against Western science, which was used in the West to discredit him.

fuentes/knorozov-1952/por_que_importa.texto: It is the founding text of the decipherment of Maya writing. Thompson rejected it, and its method was only fully accepted in the 1970s and 1980s.

fuentes/berlin-1958/soporte.texto: Article in the Journal de la Société des Américanistes, volume 47

fuentes/berlin-1958/resumen.texto: Article in which Heinrich Berlin showed that certain glyphs were repeated in the inscriptions of a single city and changed from one city to another, and called them “emblem glyphs.” He proposed that they named the cities or their dynasties.

fuentes/berlin-1958/por_que_importa.texto: It opened the way to the political geography of the Maya Classic period: with the emblem glyphs it became possible to tell which city mentioned which.

fuentes/proskouriakoff-1960/titulo.texto: Historical Implications of a Pattern of Dates at Piedras Negras, Guatemala

fuentes/proskouriakoff-1960/soporte.texto: Article in American Antiquity, volume 25, number 4

fuentes/proskouriakoff-1960/resumen.texto: Proskouriakoff grouped the stelae of Piedras Negras into series that each lasted the span of a human life, and showed that each series began with an accession date preceded by a birth date. She concluded that the inscriptions recorded the lives of rulers and not only calendars and gods.

fuentes/proskouriakoff-1960/por_que_impo.texto: It dismantled the idea that Maya texts did not speak of history and, together with Knorozov’s method, made it possible to read the chronicles of the Classic dynasties.

fuentes/rise-and-fall-of-maya-civilizati.texto: The Rise and Fall of Maya Civilization

Synthesis of Maya civilization in which Thompson presented the Classic Maya as a peaceful society of peasants guided by astronomer priests, and explained the collapse by a peasant rebellion against that elite. It went through many editions and was the standard view for decades.
It is the best example of the idealized image of the Maya that later inscriptions and archaeology corrected: warfare, sacrifice and named kings.

fuentes/blood-of-kings/soporte.texto: Exhibition catalogue of the Kimbell Art Museum, written with Mary Ellen Miller

fuentes/blood-of-kings/resumen.texto: Book that gathered Classic Maya art read in the light of decipherment: divine kingship, ritual bloodletting, warfare to capture enemies, the torture and sacrifice of captives, and the ballgame. It argues that blood was the center of the ritual life of the nobility.

fuentes/blood-of-kings/por_que_importa.texto: It changed the public image of the Maya: after it, it was no longer possible to speak of a peaceful people. Some critics noted that it exaggerated the weight of sacrifice in everyday life.

fuentes/breaking-the-maya-code/resumen.texto: History of the decipherment of Maya writing from Landa and nineteenth-century travelers to Knorozov, Proskouriakoff, Berlin and the Palenque Round Tables. Coe, who took part in the dispute, attributes the delay in decipherment to Thompson’s authority and his rejection of phonetics.

fuentes/breaking-the-maya-code/por_que_i.texto: It is the standard reference on how Maya writing was read; its view of Thompson as an obstacle is shared by most, although some consider it partial.

fuentes/chronicle-of-the-maya-kings-and-.texto: Chronicle of the Maya Kings and Queens
Book, Thames and Hudson, written with Nikolai Grube; second edition in 2008

Dynastic history of eleven Classic Maya kingdoms (Tikal, Dos Pilas, Naranjo, Caracol, Calakmul, Yaxchilan, Piedras Negras, Palenque, Tonina, Copan and Quirigua) based on the inscriptions. It presents the Classic period as a rivalry between two hegemonies, Tikal and Calakmul, with their networks of vassals, wars and captures.
It is the standard reference on Maya political history; the model of the two superpowers is broadly accepted, although how centralized those hegemonies were is debated.

fuentes/fall-of-the-ancient-maya/titulo.texto: The Fall of the Ancient Maya

fuentes/fall-of-the-ancient-maya/resumen.texto: Synthesis by the archaeologist David Webster on the Classic collapse. He argues that there was not a single cause but a combination of population excessive for agricultural capacity, environmental degradation, endemic warfare among the elites and the failure of divine kingship, with drought as an aggravating factor.

fuentes/fall-of-the-ancient-maya/por_que.texto: It is one of the most cited overall explanations of the collapse and a critique of single-cause versions.

fuentes/ancient-maya-demarest/titulo.texto: The Ancient Maya: The Rise and Fall of a Rainforest Civilization

fuentes/ancient-maya-demarest/resumen.texto: Synthesis of Maya civilization that emphasizes adaptation to the rainforest, the ritual economy of kings, and warfare. Drawing on excavations at Petexbatun and Cancuen, he argues that in western Peten the collapse began with endemic warfare between dynasties, before drought.

fuentes/ancient-maya-demarest/por_que_im.texto: It represents the position of those who give warfare and politics a central role in the collapse.

fuentes/ambivalent-conquests/titulo.texto: Ambivalent Conquests: Maya and Spaniards in Yucatan, 1517–1570

fuentes/ambivalent-conquests/resumen.texto: Study of the conquest of Yucatan and the Franciscan campaign, focused on the idolatry proceedings of 1562. Using the documents edited by Scholes and Adams, it reconstructs the torture, the confessions and the conflict among Landa, Bishop Toral, the encomenderos and Maya lords, and discusses what is true in the confessions of human sacrifice in churches.

fuentes/ambivalent-conquests/por_que_imp.texto: It is the standard analysis of the auto de fe of Maní; it neither absolves Landa nor dismisses without examination what the Maya declared.

fuentes/hodell-1995-clima-y-colapso/titu.texto: Possible Role of Climate in the Collapse of Classic Maya Civilization

fuentes/hodell-1995-clima-y-colapso/auto.texto: David A. Hodell, Jason H. Curtis and Mark Brenner

fuentes/hodell-1995-clima-y-colapso/resu.texto: Study of sediments from Lake Chichancanab, in Yucatan, whose oxygen isotopes and gypsum indicate that between 800 and 1000 came the driest period in several millennia. The authors proposed that this drought may have contributed to the Classic collapse.

fuentes/hodell-1995-clima-y-colapso/por_.texto: It began the line of climate studies of the Maya collapse, which other records of droughts in the 9th and 10th centuries later confirmed; how much weight drought carried against warfare and politics is still debated.

fuentes/kennett-2012-clima-y-politica-ma.texto: Development and Dissolution of Maya Political Systems in Response to Climate Change

Reconstruction of two thousand years of rainfall from a stalagmite in Yok Balum Cave, in Belize, compared with the dates of the inscriptions. Wet periods coincide with the rise of the Classic dynasties; increasing dryness between 660 and 1000 coincides with more recorded wars and political fragmentation, and a prolonged drought between 1020 and 1100 with the final stage of depopulation.
It joins climate data and warfare data on the same timescale and is one of the main supports for explanations that combine drought and conflict.

fuentes/canuto-2018-lidar/titulo.texto: The Complexity of Maya Lowlands Revealed by Airborne Laser Scanning of Northern Guatemala

fuentes/canuto-2018-lidar/autor.texto: Marcello A. Canuto, Francisco Estrada-Belli, Thomas G. Garrison et al.

fuentes/canuto-2018-lidar/soporte.texto: Article in Science, volume 361; survey by the LiDAR Initiative of the PACUNAM foundation

fuentes/canuto-2018-lidar/resumen.texto: Result of airborne laser scanning of more than 2,100 square kilometers of the Peten, which revealed more than sixty thousand structures hidden beneath the jungle, causeways, fields, canals and many fortifications. The authors estimate a Late Classic population of between seven and eleven million people in the Maya lowlands.

fuentes/canuto-2018-lidar/por_que_import.texto: It showed a population density, agricultural works and military defenses far greater than was assumed; the population figures are estimates and are debated.

fuentes/sugiyama-2005-templo-de-la-serpi.texto: Human Sacrifice, Militarism, and Rulership at the Feathered Serpent Pyramid, Teotihuacan

Study of the excavations of the 1980s and 1990s at the Feathered Serpent Pyramid, in which Sugiyama took part. It describes the pits with more than one hundred sacrificed individuals placed when the building was constructed, arranged in groups, many with their hands tied behind their backs and with necklaces of human jaws or imitation shell, and interprets them as an assertion of the state’s military power.
It is the main source on the mass sacrifice at Teotihuacan and proof that this practice in central Mexico is much earlier than the Mexica.

fuentes/recuerdos-del-futuro/soporte.texto: Book, Econ publishers; translated into dozens of languages

fuentes/recuerdos-del-futuro/resumen.texto: Bestselling book arguing that beings from other planets visited Earth in antiquity and inspired monuments and religions. Its examples include the sarcophagus lid of Pakal at Palenque, which it interprets as an astronaut in a spacecraft. The hieroglyphic texts of the tomb name Pakal, give the dates of his birth and death, and describe his entry into the underworld, a scene that appears on other Maya pieces.

fuentes/recuerdos-del-futuro/por_que_imp.texto: It is the origin of the most widespread version of the “ancient astronaut” theory about Mesoamerica. Archaeologists and epigraphers reject it because it ignores what the inscriptions say and assumes that Indigenous peoples could not have built their own works.

fuentes/arte-de-la-lengua-de-michoacan/t.texto: Arte de la lengua de Michuacan

fuentes/arte-de-la-lengua-de-michoacan/s.texto: Printed in Mexico by Juan Pablos

fuentes/arte-de-la-lengua-de-michoacan/r.texto: Grammar of the Purepecha language written by the Franciscan Maturino Gilberti to teach it to friars, followed the next year by a Vocabulario en lengua de Mechuacan. It describes a language with no known relatives among the other languages of Mesoamerica.

fuentes/arte-de-la-lengua-de-michoacan/p.texto: It is one of the first grammars of an American language printed in the Americas and the basis for the study of Purepecha, which more than one hundred thousand people speak today.

fuentes/arte-en-lengua-zapoteca/soporte.texto: Printed in Mexico by Pedro Balli; its Vocabulario en lengua çapoteca was published the same year

fuentes/arte-en-lengua-zapoteca/resumen.texto: Grammar of the Zapotec of the Oaxaca valley written by the Dominican Juan de Córdova, which includes a description of the 260-day Zapotec ritual calendar and its divinatory uses. He wrote it to train the friars who preached in that language.

fuentes/arte-en-lengua-zapoteca/por_que_.texto: It is the main source on sixteenth-century Zapotec and one of the few descriptions of the Zapotec calendar made while it was still in use.

fuentes/arte-en-lengua-mixteca/soporte.texto: Printed in Mexico by Pedro Balli

fuentes/arte-en-lengua-mixteca/resumen.texto: Grammar of Mixtec written by the Dominican Antonio de los Reyes, whose prologue records Mixtec traditions about the origin of the lords at Apoala and the names of the towns of the Mixteca. It was published the same year as Francisco de Alvarado’s Vocabulario en lengua mixteca.

fuentes/arte-en-lengua-mixteca/por_que_i.texto: Together with the codices, it is one of the bases for reading the history and geography of the Mixtec lordships.

fuentes/theologia-indorum/soporte.texto: Manuscript preserved in several sixteenth-century copies

fuentes/theologia-indorum/resumen.texto: Extensive exposition of Christian doctrine written in K'iche' by the Dominican Domingo de Vico, who adapted terms of the highland Maya religion to the Christian faith. It circulated in manuscript copies among the K'iche', Kaqchikel and Tz'utujil peoples.

fuentes/theologia-indorum/por_que_import.texto: It is the first major theological work written in a Maya language. Some researchers argue that the K'iche' authors of the Popol Vuh knew it and wrote in part in response to it.

personas/chak-tok-ichaak-i/resumen.texto: King of Tikal. According to Stela 31 of Tikal and other inscriptions, he died on the same day in January 378 on which Siyaj K'ak', an envoy from central Mexico, arrived in the city; most epigraphers interpret it as a violent death in the capture of the city.

personas/jatzom-kuuj/resumen.texto: Ruler of a foreign place, probably Teotihuacan, who appears in the inscriptions of Tikal as the father of Yax Nuun Ahiin I and as the lord under whose sign Siyaj K'ak' arrived in 378. His name is written with an owl and a spear-thrower, Teotihuacan emblems; his exact identity is debated.

personas/siyaj-kak/resumen.texto: Warrior chief who arrived at Tikal in January 378, in an “entrada” also recorded at El Peru and Uaxactun. After his arrival King Chak Tok Ich'aak I died and Yax Nuun Ahiin I, son of Owl Spearthrower, was enthroned; the inscriptions show him as lord of several cities in the Peten.

personas/yax-nuun-ahiin-i/resumen.texto: King of Tikal enthroned in 379, after the arrival of Siyaj K'ak’, son of Owl Spearthrower. On Stela 31, which his son commissioned, he appears on the sides dressed as a Teotihuacan warrior, with spear-thrower and shield.

personas/sihyaj-chan-kawiil-ii/resumen.texto: King of Tikal, son of Yax Nuun Ahiin I, who dedicated Stela 31 in 445. On it he presents himself as heir both to the ancient local dynasty and to the newcomers linked to Teotihuacan.

personas/yuknoom-cheen-ii/resumen.texto: King of the Snake dynasty (Kaanul) based at Calakmul, the most powerful ruler of the Maya lowlands in the 7th century. Inscriptions from other cities, such as Dos Pilas, Naranjo and Cancuen, name him as lord of their kings, and in 657 his forces attacked Tikal and forced its king to flee.

personas/yuknoom-yichaak-kahk/resumen.texto: King of Calakmul, successor of Yuknoom Ch'een II. In August 695 he was defeated by Jasaw Chan K'awiil I of Tikal, according to the lintels of Temple I at Tikal; after that date he stops appearing in the inscriptions.

personas/nuun-ujol-chaak/resumen.texto: King of Tikal who suffered attacks from Calakmul and war with his kinsman B'alaj Chan K'awiil of Dos Pilas. The Hieroglyphic Stairway 2 of Dos Pilas records his defeat in 679; he probably died in it.

personas/jasaw-chan-kawiil-i/resumen.texto: King of Tikal, son of Nuun Ujol Chaak, who in 695 defeated Yuknoom Yich'aak K'ahk’ of Calakmul and ended more than a century of subordination of his city. He is buried in Temple I, whose wooden lintels record that victory.

personas/balaj-chan-kawiil/resumen.texto: Prince of the Tikal dynasty who ruled Dos Pilas and switched to the side of Calakmul, of which he declared himself a vassal. With that support he waged war on Tikal and on its king Nuun Ujol Chaak, probably his brother, whom he defeated in 679, according to the Hieroglyphic Stairway of Dos Pilas.

personas/wak-chanil-ajaw/resumen.texto: Daughter of B'alaj Chan K'awiil of Dos Pilas, she arrived at Naranjo in 682 to refound her dynasty and governed it de facto during her son’s minority. Her stelae show her standing on captives and record campaigns against neighboring cities.

personas/kinich-janaab-pakal/resumen.texto: King of Palenque from the age of twelve until his death, one of the best-documented Classic Maya rulers. He rebuilt the city after the attacks by Calakmul in 599 and 611; his tomb, beneath the Temple of the Inscriptions, was found by Alberto Ruz in 1952.

personas/kinich-yax-kuk-mo/resumen.texto: Founder of the dynasty of sixteen kings of Copan in 426, remembered on Altar Q. The inscriptions link him with Teotihuacan and the central Peten, and isotope analysis of the bones from the tomb attributed to him indicates that he was not raised in Copan.

personas/uaxaclajuun-ubaah-kawiil/resume.texto: Thirteenth king of Copan, who erected much of the stelae of the Great Plaza. In 738 he was captured and beheaded by K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat, lord of Quirigua, who had been his vassal, according to the stelae of Quirigua.

personas/kak-tiliw-chan-yopaat/resumen.texto: King of Quirigua, placed on the throne under the authority of Copan, who in 738 captured and sacrificed his lord, Waxaklajuun Ub'aah K'awiil. His stelae, among them Stela E, more than ten meters tall, celebrate that victory and the independence of his city.

personas/itzamnaaj-bahlam-iii/resumen.texto: King of Yaxchilan for about sixty years, who expanded the city and had himself depicted capturing enemies. He commissioned Lintels 24 to 26 of Structure 23, dedicated to his wife K'ab'al Xook.

personas/kabal-xook/resumen.texto: Principal wife of Itzamnaaj B'alam III of Yaxchilan. Lintels 24 and 25 show her drawing a cord with thorns through her tongue in a bloodletting rite, and before a vision serpent, one of the best-known representations of Maya autosacrifice.

personas/ocho-venado/resumen.texto: Mixtec lord of Tilantongo whose life is recounted in the Zouche-Nuttall, Bodley and Colombino-Becker codices. According to those paintings he unified much of the Mixteca by conquest and alliances, had rival lords captured and sacrificed, and was himself captured and sacrificed in 1115 by Four Wind, of an enemy lineage.

personas/ce-acatl-topiltzin/resumen.texto: Ruler of Tula according to Nahua traditions recorded after the conquest, which present him as a priest of Quetzalcóatl, opposed to human sacrifice and expelled from the city. No contemporary inscription confirms it: his story mixes tradition and myth, and the sources do not agree on the dates.

personas/tariacuri/resumen.texto: Founder of the Purepecha royal lineage of the Uacúsecha according to the Relación de Michoacán, which recounts how he united the peoples of Lake Pátzcuaro by war and alliances and divided the lordship between his son and his nephews. He is known only through that tradition, written two centuries later.

personas/tzitzipandaquare/resumen.texto: Cazonci or Purepecha king based at Tzintzuntzan, who expanded the kingdom to the west and south. In his time the Purepecha defeated the Mexica army of the tlatoani Axayácatl near Taximaroa (1478–1479).

personas/nachi-cocom/resumen.texto: Maya lord of the province of Sotuta, of the Cocom lineage that had governed Mayapan. According to Landa and Gaspar Antonio Chi, in 1536 he had the embassy of the Xiu of Maní killed at Otzmal. He resisted the Montejo, was defeated in 1542 near T'ho (Mérida) and, once baptized, became one of Landa’s informants.

personas/gaspar-antonio-chi/resumen.texto: Maya noble of Maní, of the Xiu lineage through his mother, educated by the Franciscans. He served as general interpreter for the government of Yucatan, as an informant to Landa, and as the author of an account of ancient customs included in the geographical relations of 1581–1582.

personas/diego-de-landa/resumen.texto: Spanish Franciscan who arrived in Yucatan in 1549, learned Yucatec Maya and, as provincial, directed in 1562 the idolatry trials of Maní, with torture of thousands of Maya and the burning of images and books. Tried in Spain for these excesses and acquitted in 1569, he wrote around 1566 the Relación de las cosas de Yucatán and returned as bishop in 1573.

personas/francisco-de-toral/resumen.texto: Spanish Franciscan, the first resident bishop of Yucatan, who arrived in August 1562 in the midst of Landa’s campaign. He reviewed the Maní trials, freed prisoners, denounced the torture to the Crown and secured Landa’s dispatch to Spain.

personas/jeronimo-de-alcala/resumen.texto: Spanish Franciscan to whom the Relación de Michoacán is attributed, compiled between 1539 and 1541 for viceroy Antonio de Mendoza from what elders and Purepecha priests had told. The text presents him as interpreter and compiler, not as the author of what it narrates.

personas/maturino-gilberti/resumen.texto: French Franciscan who spent more than forty years in Michoacan and published in Mexico the first printed grammar (1558) and the first vocabulary (1559) of the Purepecha language. His Diálogo de doctrina cristiana in that language (1559) was held back and examined for years by ecclesiastical authorities over doctrinal doubts.

personas/domingo-de-vico/resumen.texto: Dominican born in Jaén who arrived in Guatemala in 1544 in the group of Bartolomé de las Casas. He learned several Maya languages and wrote the Theologia Indorum in K'iche'; he was killed in 1555 by Lacandon and Ch'ol people of Acalá whom he was trying to evangelize.

personas/francisco-ximenez/resumen.texto: Dominican born in Écija who worked in Guatemala and learned K'iche', Kaqchikel and Tz'utujil. While priest of Chichicastenango he copied and translated into Spanish, around 1701–1703, the K'iche' manuscript of the Popol Vuh, the only version that survives.

personas/john-lloyd-stephens/resumen.texto: American diplomat and traveler who toured the Maya ruins with Frederick Catherwood between 1839 and 1842. His books argued that the cities had been built by the ancestors of the Maya who lived there, against the theories of Egyptians, Israelites or Atlanteans then in fashion.

personas/frederick-catherwood/resumen.texto: English draftsman and architect who accompanied Stephens. His drawings of Copan, Palenque, Uxmal and other cities, made partly with the camera lucida, were so accurate that epigraphers still use them.

personas/charles-etienne-brasseur-de-bou.texto: French priest and Americanist who found and published key texts: the Rabinal Achí (1862), the Popol Vuh in French (1861), the copy of Landa’s Relación in Madrid (1864) and part of the Madrid Codex (the Troano). In his last years he interpreted these texts as evidence of Atlantis, ideas that no one holds today.

personas/ernst-forstemann/resumen.texto: Librarian of the Royal Library in Dresden who studied the Maya codex of his institution. Between 1880 and 1906 he explained the vigesimal number system, the Long Count and the Venus tables of the codex, the calendrical part of Maya writing.

personas/edward-herbert-thompson/resumen.texto: American consul in Yucatan who bought the hacienda where Chichen Itza stood and between 1904 and 1910 dredged the Sacred Cenote. He removed human bones, gold, jade and copal, much of which he sent to Harvard’s Peabody Museum, which led to a long lawsuit with the Mexican government.

personas/sylvanus-morley/resumen.texto: American archaeologist who directed, for the Carnegie Institution, the restoration of Chichen Itza and recorded hundreds of inscriptions. He spread the image of the Classic Maya as a peaceful people ruled by astronomer priests, an image that the murals of Bonampak and decipherment refuted.

personas/j-eric-s-thompson/resumen.texto: British Mayanist, the greatest authority on Maya writing in the mid-20th century, who advanced the study of calendars and glyphs but maintained that writing was not phonetic and that the inscriptions did not speak of history. He rejected Knorozov’s work harshly; Michael Coe attributes this rejection partly to his anticommunism and argues that his authority delayed acceptance of the decipherment.

personas/alfonso-caso/resumen.texto: Mexican archaeologist who excavated Monte Albán from 1931 and in 1932 found Tomb 7, with a Mixtec burial goods of gold, silver, jade and carved bone. He established the sequence of Monte Albán and advanced the reading of the Mixtec codices and of Eight Deer’s life.

personas/matthew-stirling/resumen.texto: Smithsonian archaeologist who excavated Tres Zapotes, La Venta and San Lorenzo between 1938 and 1946. He found several colossal heads and Stela C of Tres Zapotes, and argued that the Olmec culture was earlier than the Maya, something radiocarbon dating confirmed.

personas/alberto-ruz-lhuillier/resumen.texto: Mexican archaeologist born in Paris who directed the excavations of Palenque. In 1948–1949 he found the sealed stairway of the Temple of the Inscriptions and in 1952 reached the crypt with Pakal’s sarcophagus.

personas/yuri-knorozov/resumen.texto: Soviet linguist who in 1952, working in Leningrad with reproductions of the codices and Landa’s “alphabet,” showed that Maya writing combined word signs and syllabic signs. His method was rejected in the West for two decades and is the basis of present-day decipherment.

personas/tatiana-proskouriakoff/resumen.texto: Architect and Mayanist born in Russia and raised in the United States, who worked for the Carnegie Institution and the Peabody Museum. In 1960 she showed, with the dates of the stelae of Piedras Negras, that the inscriptions recorded the lives of royal rulers: births, accessions, captures and deaths.

personas/linda-schele/resumen.texto: American epigrapher who, at the first Palenque Round Table (1973), reconstructed with Peter Mathews the city’s list of kings. With Mary Miller she wrote The Blood of Kings (1986), which placed sacrifice, autosacrifice and warfare at the center of the image of the Maya.

personas/michael-d-coe/resumen.texto: American archaeologist who excavated San Lorenzo with Richard Diehl, early defended Knorozov’s method and wrote the history of the decipherment, Breaking the Maya Code (1992). He presented the Grolier Codex at a New York exhibition in 1971 and in 2016 signed the study that defended its authenticity.

personas/simon-martin/resumen.texto: British epigrapher and curator of the Penn Museum, who with Nikolai Grube reconstructed the political history of the Classic Maya as a system of rival kingdoms headed by Tikal and Calakmul.

personas/nikolai-grube/resumen.texto: German epigrapher, professor in Bonn, co-author with Simon Martin of the Chronicle of the Maya Kings and Queens (2000) and excavator of Uxul and other sites in Campeche.

personas/arthur-demarest/resumen.texto: American archaeologist at Vanderbilt University who directed the Petexbatun (Dos Pilas, Aguateca) and Cancuen projects. He argues that endemic warfare played a central role in the collapse of the Pasión region, against those who emphasize drought.

personas/inga-clendinnen/resumen.texto: Australian historian who studied the conquest of Yucatan and the 1562 idolatry trials in Ambivalent Conquests (1987), and Mexica society in Aztecs (1991).

personas/william-saturno/resumen.texto: American archaeologist who in 2001 discovered the murals of San Bartolo (Guatemala), from the 1st century BC, and in 2012 the astronomical tables painted in a house at Xultún.

hechos/cultura-olmeca/resumen.texto: Culture of southern Veracruz and Tabasco that created, between around 1600 and 400 BC, the first great centers of Mesoamerica (San Lorenzo, La Venta, Tres Zapotes), with colossal heads of rulers and a style that spread as far as Morelos, Guerrero and Chiapas. At the El Manatí sanctuary the oldest known rubber balls were found together with wooden busts and bones of newborns that their excavators interpret as sacrificial offerings. Whether it was a “mother culture” of the later ones or one of several contemporary cultures is an open debate.

hechos/juego-de-pelota-mesoamericano/res.texto: Ritual game played with a solid rubber ball struck with the hip, practiced throughout Mesoamerica: the oldest known court, at Paso de la Amada (Chiapas), dates from around 1650 BC. It had religious and political meaning and in some places ended in the sacrifice of players, as the reliefs of El Tajín and Chichen Itza show; it was also a sport and an occasion for betting. The Spaniards saw it played in the 16th century, and a variant, the ulama, survives in Sinaloa.

hechos/cuenta-larga/resumen.texto: Calendar that counts the days elapsed since a mythical starting date equivalent to August 11, 3114 BC, used together with the 260-day ritual cycle and the 365-day year. The oldest known dates are from the 1st century BC, at Chiapa de Corzo (36 BC) and Tres Zapotes (32 BC), outside the Maya area; the Classic Maya carved them on their monuments until 909. The end of the 13th b’ak’tun, in December 2012, gave rise to a modern prophecy with no basis in the inscriptions.

hechos/escritura-maya/resumen.texto: The most complete writing system of pre-Columbian America: it combines word signs and syllabic signs and could write any phrase of the language. It was used since at least 300 BC, as the texts of San Bartolo show, until after the conquest, on stone, stucco, ceramics and bark-paper books, of which four survive. The friars pursued the books as idolatry, and writing ceased to be used toward the end of the 17th century; today it is largely readable.

hechos/cultura-zapoteca/resumen.texto: People of the central valleys of Oaxaca who founded, around 500 BC at Monte Albán, one of the first city-states of Mesoamerica, with its own writing and calendar. Its first monuments show enemies killed or sacrificed, and the expansion of Monte Albán into neighboring regions was recorded on conquest slabs. After Monte Albán was abandoned, the Postclassic Zapotec lordships, such as Zaachila and Tehuantepec, competed with the Mixtecs and resisted the Mexica; today they remain one of the most populous Indigenous peoples of Mexico.

hechos/civilizacion-maya/resumen.texto: Civilization of the Maya-speaking peoples of southeastern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and western Honduras and El Salvador, with farming villages from around 1000 BC, cities from the Preclassic, its peak in the Classic (250–900) and kingdoms in the Postclassic until the Spanish conquest, which ended with the fall of the Itza of Nojpetén in 1697. It was never a single empire but a mosaic of kingdoms with shared writing, calendar, astronomy and architecture, often at war with one another. The Maya did not disappear: several million people speak today one of the some thirty Maya languages.

hechos/apogeo-de-el-mirador/titulo.texto: El Mirador and the Preclassic Maya collapse

hechos/apogeo-de-el-mirador/resumen.texto: Between 300 BC and AD 150 the Maya of northern Peten built enormous pyramids linked by causeways at El Mirador, Nakbé and other centers, centuries before the Classic. Around the 2nd century these cities were abandoned in what is called the Preclassic collapse; deforestation, soil erosion that filled the bajos, and droughts have been proposed as causes, without agreement among specialists.

hechos/fundacion-de-monte-alban/resumen.texto: Around 500 BC the Zapotecs of the Oaxaca valley partly left San José Mogote and other villages and founded a new capital on top of an uninhabited hill in the center of the valley. Kent Flannery and Joyce Marcus interpret it as the union of rival communities in a neutral place that was easy to defend; the city grew rapidly and within a few centuries dominated the valley.

hechos/erupcion-del-xitle/titulo.texto: Eruption of Xitle and abandonment of Cuicuilco

hechos/erupcion-del-xitle/resumen.texto: Eruption of the Xitle volcano, in the south of the Valley of Mexico, which covered Cuicuilco and what is today the Pedregal de San Ángel with lava. Radiocarbon dates it between 245 and 315, although other authors date it before the Common Era; the depopulation of Cuicuilco reinforced the growth of Teotihuacan.

hechos/sacrificios-del-templo-de-la-serp.texto: Sacrifices at the Feathered Serpent Pyramid of Teotihuacan

When the Feathered Serpent Pyramid of Teotihuacan was built, around 200, some 200 sacrificed people were buried beneath and around the building, according to the excavations of the 1980s and 1990s directed by Rubén Cabrera, Saburo Sugiyama and George Cowgill, which recovered more than one hundred. They were arranged in groups of numbers with calendrical meaning, many with their hands tied behind their backs, dressed as warriors and wearing necklaces of human jaws; isotope analyses indicate that many had not been raised in the city. Their excavators interpret them as soldiers or captives sacrificed to consecrate the power of the state.

hechos/caida-de-teotihuacan/resumen.texto: Around 550 the temples and palaces along the Avenue of the Dead at Teotihuacan were burned and their sculptures smashed, while the residential neighborhoods suffered less; the exact date is debated. Most archaeologists interpret it as an internal revolt against the elite, after a period of decline, rather than as an invasion. The city remained inhabited but lost its power, which passed to centers such as Xochicalco, Cacaxtla, Cholula and later Tula.

hechos/cultura-tolteca/resumen.texto: Tula, in Hidalgo, was the capital of a state that dominated part of central Mexico between 900 and 1150, with pillars in the form of warriors, walls of serpents devouring skeletons and a tzompantli. The Mexica and other Nahua peoples remembered the Toltecs as inventors of the arts and a model of legitimacy, and colonial chronicles mix that memory with myths, such as that of Ce Ácatl Topiltzin Quetzalcóatl. The similarities between Tula and Chichen Itza were first explained as a Toltec conquest of Yucatan; today many think of exchanges in both directions, and the question remains debated.

hechos/cultura-mixteca/resumen.texto: People of the Mixteca (Oaxaca, Guerrero and Puebla), organized into dozens of lordships governed by related lineages, whose roughly five centuries of history are recorded in painted codices. They were great goldsmiths and painters; in the Postclassic they spread into the central valleys of Oaxaca and the coast, where Tututepec formed a powerful kingdom, and in the 15th century part of their territory came to pay tribute to the Mexica.

hechos/conquistas-de-ocho-venado/resumen.texto: According to the Zouche-Nuttall, Bodley and Colombino-Becker codices, Eight Deer, lord of Tilantongo, conquered and subjected dozens of Mixtec towns at the end of the 11th century, allied himself with a Toltec-Chichimec lord who pierced his nose as a sign of rank, and sacrificed captured rival lords. In 1115 he was captured and sacrificed by his enemies. It is the most detailed biography of a Mesoamerican ruler before the Mexica.

hechos/pueblo-totonaca/resumen.texto: People of the central coast of Veracruz and the northern highlands of Puebla, the Totonacapan, whose main city in the 16th century was Cempoala. The Mexica had subjected them to tribute in the 15th century; in 1519 the Totonacs of Cempoala allied with Hernán Cortés against Mexica tax collectors and gave him warriors and porters. Whether they were the builders of El Tajín is debated.

hechos/pueblo-huasteco/resumen.texto: Maya-speaking people of the northern Gulf coast, the Huasteca, separated from the rest of the Maya for about three thousand years, with its own style of sculpture and ceramics in the Postclassic. The Mexica conquered part of their territory in the 15th century and took Huastec captives to be sacrificed in Tenochtitlan; after the Spanish conquest, Nuño de Guzmán, governor of Pánuco from 1527, enslaved thousands of them and sold them in the Antilles.

hechos/pueblos-chichimecas/resumen.texto: “Chichimeca” was the name the Nahuas gave to the peoples of the north, hunter-gatherers or farmers of Aridoamerica such as the Guachichil, Guamare, Pame and Zacateco, whom they regarded as people without cities, and at the same time the origin that several noble lineages of the center took pride in. From the 10th century the northern frontier of Mesoamerica withdrew southward, with the abandonment of centers such as La Quemada. Their war against the Spaniards and their Indigenous allies in the 16th century is the Chichimec War.

hechos/estado-purepecha/resumen.texto: Kingdom with its capital at Tzintzuntzan which in the 14th and 15th centuries unified western Mexico by war, with a language that has no known relatives and an advanced copper and bronze metallurgy. According to the Relación de Michoacán, war was a religious duty to bring firewood and captives to the god Curicaueri, and prisoners were sacrificed or kept as slaves. It halted the Mexica expansion, submitted to the Spaniards in 1522, and lost its last king, Tangáxuan II, executed by Nuño de Guzmán in 1530.

hechos/guerra-purepecha-mexica/resumen.texto: Around 1478–1479 the Mexica tlatoani Axayácatl invaded the Purepecha kingdom and was defeated near Taximaroa by the army of Tzitzipandáquare. Diego Durán’s chronicle, written a century later with Mexica informants, describes a defeat with thousands dead, figures that cannot be verified. From then on the two states fortified their border and remained in intermittent war; in 1520 the Purepecha refused to help Tenochtitlan against the Spaniards.

hechos/entrada-de-siyaj-kak-en-tikal/tit.texto: Arrival of Siyaj K'ak' at Tikal

hechos/entrada-de-siyaj-kak-en-tikal/res.texto: In January 378 Siyaj K'ak', a warrior chief linked with Teotihuacan, arrived at Tikal, according to Stela 31 and other texts that record his passage through El Perú a few days earlier. That same day King Chak Tok Ich'aak I died, and a year later Yax Nuun Ahiin I, son of Owl Spearthrower, was enthroned. What is documented is the change of dynasty and the arrival of Teotihuacan symbols in the Petén; whether it was a military conquest from central Mexico, as David Stuart argues, or an intervention by Maya groups allied with Teotihuacan, is debated.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-dinastia-de-copan.texto: In 426 K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo' received the insignia of kingship in a place associated with Teotihuacan, and the following year he arrived at Copan, according to Altar Q and other texts; he founded a dynasty of sixteen kings that lasted almost four centuries. Beneath the Acropolis a tomb attributed to him was found, with Teotihuacan elements, and the isotopes of his bones indicate that he was raised far from Copan.

hechos/guerras-entre-tikal-y-calakmul/re.texto: Wars of the 6th to 8th centuries between Tikal and the Snake dynasty (Kaanul) of Calakmul with its allies, which the inscriptions record as captures, “star wars” and changes of vassalage. Calakmul defeated Tikal in 562 with Caracol, attacked it again in 657 and supported Dos Pilas in its war against it; Tikal recovered with the victory of 695 and in 743–744 defeated El Perú and Naranjo, allies of Calakmul. Simon Martin and Nikolai Grube interpret them as the rivalry of two hegemonies that organized the Classic Maya world.

hechos/derrota-de-tikal-en-562/titulo.texto: Defeat of Tikal by Caracol and Calakmul in 562

hechos/derrota-de-tikal-en-562/resumen.texto: In 562 Tikal suffered a “star war” at the hands of Caracol, an ally of Calakmul, recorded on Altar 21 of Caracol; its king Wak Chan K'awiil was probably captured and sacrificed. For more than a century Tikal almost erected no monuments, a period that archaeologists call “the hiatus.”

hechos/ataques-de-calakmul-a-palenque/re.texto: In 599 and 611 Calakmul attacked Palenque, according to the panels of the Temple of the Inscriptions, which record the defeat and the fall of the city’s gods. Pakal, who came to the throne in 615 at the age of twelve, rebuilt Palenque’s power in the following decades.

hechos/guerra-entre-dos-pilas-y-tikal/ti.texto: War between Dos Pilas and Tikal

hechos/guerra-entre-dos-pilas-y-tikal/re.texto: War between two branches of the Tikal dynasty: B'alaj Chan K'awiil, king of Dos Pilas, declared himself a vassal of Calakmul and fought against Nuun Ujol Chaak of Tikal. According to the Hieroglyphic Stairway 2 of Dos Pilas, he was defeated and fled several times until, with Calakmul’s support, he defeated Tikal in 679, in a battle that the text describes with piles of skulls and pools of blood.

hechos/victoria-de-tikal-sobre-calakmul/.texto: In August 695 Jasaw Chan K'awiil I of Tikal defeated Yuknoom Yich'aak K'ahk’ of Calakmul, according to the wooden lintels of Temple I, the building where he was buried. The victory ended Tikal’s subordination and marked the beginning of Calakmul’s decline as a power.

hechos/toma-de-palenque-por-tonina/titul.texto: Toniná captures the king of Palenque

hechos/toma-de-palenque-por-tonina/resum.texto: In 711 Toniná captured the king of Palenque K'inich K'an Joy Chitam II, who appears bound as a captive on a relief from Toniná. It is not known whether he was sacrificed: later texts from Palenque may indicate that he returned to the throne.

hechos/captura-de-waxaklajuun-ubaah-kawi.texto: Quirigua captures and sacrifices the king of Copan

In 738 K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat of Quirigua, who governed as a vassal of Copan, captured his lord Waxaklajuun Ub'aah K'awiil and had him beheaded, according to the stelae of Quirigua. Quirigua became independent and grew with the trade of the Motagua valley; Copan kept its dynasty, but the Hieroglyphic Stairway of 755 is interpreted as an attempt to restore its prestige.

hechos/guerras-del-petexbatun/resumen.texto: From 761, when Dos Pilas was defeated by Tamarindito, the Petexbatun region broke up into wars among small lordships. The Vanderbilt University project directed by Arthur Demarest found walls built with stones from the palaces, fortified villages and the depopulation of the area; Aguateca, the last refuge of the dynasty, was attacked and burned around 810. Demarest presents it as a case in which endemic warfare preceded any environmental crisis.

hechos/matanza-de-cancuen/resumen.texto: Around 800 the royal family and nobility of Cancuen were massacred: in 2005 the team of Arthur Demarest and Tomás Barrientos announced the discovery of some three dozen bodies of men, women and children, with their jade and shell ornaments, thrown into a palace cistern with spear and axe marks, and nearby, the tomb of King Kan Maax and his wife. The city was abandoned at once; who the attackers were is not known.

hechos/guerra-en-el-mundo-maya/resumen.texto: Archaeology and decipherment have shown that warfare was frequent in the Maya world: inscriptions record captures of kings and nobles, attacks on cities (“star wars”) and changes of vassalage, and images show captives tortured and sacrificed, as at Bonampak, Toniná and Yaxchilan. People fought with spears, spear-throwers and shields and sought to take captives, but cities were also burned and tombs desecrated, and lidar revealed walls, ditches and fortresses. Landa and other 16th-century sources describe Postclassic wars over land, tribute and slaves.

hechos/sacrificio-humano-maya/titulo.texto: Human sacrifice and autosacrifice among the Maya

hechos/sacrificio-humano-maya/resumen.texto: The Maya practiced human sacrifice from the Preclassic until the conquest, and their nobility practiced blood autosacrifice of the tongue, the ears or the penis. Classic images show mainly the beheading and heart extraction of war captives, and bones from cenotes and burials confirm sacrifices of adults and children. For the Postclassic, Landa also describes sacrifices by arrows, the throwing of people into the cenote of Chichen Itza, the flaying of the body so that a priest could dance dressed in the skin, and the sharing of the flesh of the sacrificed, which the lords and guests ate when it was not buried in the temple courtyard. Specialists usually consider its scale smaller than the one sources from central Mexico attribute to the Mexica, although the comparison is difficult.

hechos/apogeo-de-chichen-itza/resumen.texto: Between the 9th and 11th centuries Chichen Itza was the most powerful city of northern Yucatan, with the Temple of Kukulcan, the largest ballcourt in Mesoamerica, with reliefs of decapitated players, and a platform of carved skulls (tzompantli). Maya chronicles and Landa attribute its history to the Itza and to disputes among lineages, with dates that do not match; archaeology places its decline in the 11th century, although the cenote remained a place of pilgrimage.

hechos/sacrificios-en-el-cenote-sagrado/.texto: The Sacred Cenote of Chichen Itza

Landa and other 16th-century sources recount that at Chichen Itza living people and valuable objects were thrown into a large cenote as an offering to the rain gods, and that the pilgrimage continued after the city was abandoned. Edward H. Thompson dredged the cenote between 1904 and 1910 and removed gold, jade, copal, textiles and human bones, most of which he sent to Harvard’s Peabody Museum; the INAH explored it again in the 1960s. Studies of the bones identified remains of more than one hundred people, many of them children and young people, although not all of them necessarily died as sacrifices.

hechos/colapso-maya-clasico/resumen.texto: Between the late 8th and early 10th centuries the cities of the southern lowlands stopped erecting monuments and lost most of their population; the last Long Count date is from 909, at Toniná. Lake sediments and stalagmites record severe droughts in those centuries, and the inscriptions and archaeology record an increase in wars; overpopulation, deforestation and the loss of legitimacy of divine kings have also been proposed. Today it is seen as the end of the Classic system of kingdoms and not of the Maya: northern Yucatan flourished in those same centuries, and millions of Maya still live in the region.

hechos/liga-de-mayapan/titulo.texto: Mayapan and the League of Mayapan

hechos/liga-de-mayapan/resumen.texto: Mayapan was the capital of northern Yucatan from around 1220 until the mid-15th century, governed by the Cocom with lords of other provinces who, according to Landa, had to live in the city. Colonial chronicles speak of a “league” with Uxmal and Chichen Itza, whose existence as a formal alliance archaeologists doubt. It was a walled and densely settled city, a center of trade in salt, cotton cloth, cacao and slaves.

hechos/caida-de-mayapan/resumen.texto: Around the mid-15th century the lords of the provinces, led by the Xiu, rebelled against the Cocom of Mayapan and killed all members of that family except one son who was away; according to Landa, because a Cocom had brought Mexican warriors from the garrisons of Tabasco and Xicalango into the city and was enslaving common people. The Books of Chilam Balam record the destruction of the city in a katun of those years, and excavations found pits with the remains of dozens of dismembered and burned people and burned buildings from that period. Afterward Yucatan was divided into some sixteen rival provinces, the situation the Spaniards found.

hechos/esclavitud-entre-los-mayas/resume.texto: Sixteenth-century sources describe slavery in pre-conquest Yucatan: according to Landa, war captives and people condemned for theft who could not restore what they had stolen were slaves, and slaves, even children, were bought to be sacrificed. Slaves were one of the goods of long-distance trade, along with salt, cloth and cacao.

hechos/matanza-de-otzmal/resumen.texto: In 1536, in the midst of drought and famine, the lord of the Xiu of Maní and other nobles went to Chichen Itza to offer a sacrifice to the rain gods, taking slaves to throw into the cenote, and asked for passage through Sotuta, the province of their enemies the Cocom. Nachi Cocom received them at Otzmal and had them killed, out of the old enmity that dated from the fall of Mayapan: according to Landa, he lodged them in a house that he set on fire and killed those who tried to escape, and Gaspar Antonio Chi also recounts it. The enmity weighed on the conquest: the Xiu allied with the Montejo in the early 1540s, and the Cocom resisted.

hechos/reino-kiche-de-qumarkaj/resumen.texto: Kingdom of the K'iche' with its capital at Q'umarkaj which in the 15th century, especially under King K'iq'ab, dominated by conquest and tribute much of the Guatemalan highlands, until the rebellion of the Kaqchikel. The Popol Vuh and the Título de Totonicapán recount the origin of its lineages, their migrations and their wars, with the sacrifice of captives. It fell in 1524 to Pedro de Alvarado, who brought Nahua allies from central Mexico; it had at first been supported by the Kaqchikel and, according to Alvarado’s own letter to Cortés, he burned the K'iche' kings alive and set fire to the city.

hechos/fundacion-de-iximche/titulo.texto: Kaqchikel break and founding of Iximche

hechos/fundacion-de-iximche/resumen.texto: Around 1470, in the time of the K'iche' king K'iq'ab, the Kaqchikel separated from Q'umarkaj and founded their own capital at Iximche, according to the Memorial de Sololá. Decades of war between the two kingdoms followed, which in 1524 led the Kaqchikel to ally first with the Spaniards against the K'iche'.

hechos/escuelas-franciscanas-de-yucatan/.texto: Franciscan schools and town congregation in Yucatan

According to Landa, from the mid-1540s the Franciscans of Yucatan gathered the sons of Maya lords beside their convents to teach them doctrine and to read and write Yucatec Maya with Latin letters, in a grammar that was studied “like Latin”; at first some lords sent enslaved children instead of their own sons, out of fear that the friars would enslave them as the Spaniards had done. The friars, with the support of the authorities, also ordered the Maya to leave their scattered settlements and gather in towns to be catechized. From those schools came learned nobles such as Gaspar Antonio Chi and the alphabetic writing of Maya with which the Books of Chilam Balam were later written; Landa also recounts that the educated children denounced their parents’ idolatries to the friars.

hechos/tasacion-de-tomas-lopez-medel/tit.texto: Assessment of Yucatan tribute by the oidor Tomás López Medel

hechos/tasacion-de-tomas-lopez-medel/res.texto: According to Landa, around 1550 the encomenderos of Yucatan collected from the Maya all the tribute they could, without a royal assessment, and demanded personal service of every kind, even hiring them out as porters; the Franciscans appealed to Alonso López de Cerrato, president of the Audiencia of Guatemala charged with applying the New Laws, but his first assessment did not stop the abuses. At the friars’ request, the Audiencia sent the oidor Tomás López Medel, who assessed the tribute and abolished personal service, which according to Landa set the encomenderos against the Franciscans. It is a documented case of the protective laws applied in Yucatan and also of their limits: the encomenderos resisted the assessment, and complaints of abuse continued in the following decades.

hechos/auto-de-fe-de-mani/resumen.texto: In May 1562 idols and human remains were found in a cave near Maní, and the Franciscan provincial Diego de Landa, with the support of the alcalde mayor Diego Quijada, opened idolatry trials at Maní, Sotuta and Hocabá with interrogations under torture: according to the contemporary counts cited by Inga Clendinnen, some 4,500 people were tortured and 158 died, and there were also suicides and cripples. On July 12 an auto de fe was held at Maní with public punishments and the burning of idols; in his Relación Landa acknowledges that the friars burned all the hieroglyphic books they found, without saying how many or where. The confessions extracted included recent human sacrifices, some in churches, which Clendinnen considers partly credible and partly the product of torture. Bishop Francisco de Toral halted the trials and denounced the torture, and Landa was tried in Spain, where he was acquitted in 1569.

hechos/expedicion-de-stephens-y-catherwo.texto: Between 1839 and 1842 John Lloyd Stephens, a United States diplomatic envoy, and the draftsman Frederick Catherwood toured Copan, Quirigua, Palenque, Uxmal and dozens of sites in Yucatan. Their books, with very precise engravings, made Maya civilization known in the United States and Europe and argued that the ruins were the work of the ancestors of the region’s Indigenous people. Stephens bought the ruins of Copan for fifty dollars with the idea of taking monuments to New York, which he never did.

hechos/imagen-de-los-mayas-pacificos/tit.texto: The image of the peaceful Maya

hechos/imagen-de-los-mayas-pacificos/res.texto: From the 1920s and 1930s, archaeologists of the Carnegie Institution such as Sylvanus Morley and J. Eric S. Thompson spread the idea that the Classic Maya had been a peaceful people governed by priests devoted to astronomy and the calendar, unlike the Mexica. The murals of Bonampak, known since 1946, Proskouriakoff’s work of 1960 and decipherment showed named kings, wars, captures and sacrifices, and that image was abandoned in the 1970s and 1980s. It is cited as an example of how researchers’ prior ideas shape their reading of the data.

hechos/descubrimiento-de-la-tumba-de-pak.texto: When he began his excavations at Palenque in 1948–1949, Alberto Ruz noticed that a slab of the floor of the Temple of the Inscriptions had holes for lifting it, and beneath it he found a stairway filled with rubble. After four seasons of excavation he reached the crypt in June 1952, with Pakal’s sarcophagus, his jade mosaic mask and, at the entrance, the remains of five or six sacrificed young people. He showed that some Maya pyramids were built as funerary monuments for kings, and not only as temple bases.

hechos/desciframiento-de-la-escritura-ma.texto: Reading Maya writing advanced in stages: Förstemann explained the numbers and calendar of the Dresden Codex in the 1880s; Knorozov showed in 1952, with the help of Landa’s “alphabet,” that the writing was partly syllabic; Heinrich Berlin identified the emblem glyphs of the cities in 1958, and Tatiana Proskouriakoff proved in 1960 that the inscriptions narrated the lives of kings. From the Palenque Round Table of 1973, with Linda Schele, Floyd Lounsbury and Peter Mathews, and with David Stuart in the 1980s, scholars moved on to reading complete texts. According to Michael Coe, the resistance of J. Eric S. Thompson, who denied phonetics, delayed acceptance of Knorozov’s method by about two decades.

hechos/fenomeno-2012/resumen.texto: A belief spread from the 1970s by New Age authors and later by books, films and the media, according to which the Maya had prophesied the end of the world or a cosmic transformation for December 21, 2012, the end of the 13th b’ak’tun of the Long Count.
