The best-known Classic inscription that mentions that date, Monument 6 of Tortuguero, speaks of a god who would descend that day, with no announcement of catastrophe, and other inscriptions, such as those of Palenque, mention dates thousands of years later. Mayanists, NASA and Maya organizations refuted it; the date passed without anything special happening.

hechos/calaveras-de-cristal/resumen.texto: Skulls carved from rock crystal that since the 19th century have been presented as Aztec or Maya works, some with stories of supernatural powers, such as the Mitchell-Hedges skull, which its owner said was found at Lubaantun (Belize). Studies by the British Museum and the Smithsonian Institution using electron microscopes showed marks of modern lapidary wheels, and none comes from a documented excavation; several passed through the French antiquarian Eugène Boban. No specialist considers them pre-Hispanic.

lugares/san-lorenzo-tenochtitlan/resumen.texto: First great Olmec center, on an artificial plateau in southern Veracruz, with ten colossal basalt heads brought from the Tuxtla Mountains and a stone drainage system. Around 900 BC many of its monuments were mutilated and buried, for reasons that are debated, and the center passed to La Venta.

lugares/la-venta/resumen.texto: Olmec capital on an island in the swamps of Tabasco between 900 and 400 BC, with a large earthen pyramid, colossal heads, throne altars and buried offerings of jade and serpentine mosaics. Matthew Stirling excavated it in the 1940s; because of the oil industry, its monuments were moved in 1958 to La Venta Park-Museum in Villahermosa.

lugares/tres-zapotes/resumen.texto: Olmec and Epi-Olmec center in Veracruz that remained inhabited when La Venta declined. There Stela C was found, with a Long Count date corresponding to 32 BC, one of the oldest known.

lugares/tlatilco/resumen.texto: Preclassic village in the Valley of Mexico, in present-day Naucalpan, known for hundreds of burials found by brickmakers since the 1930s, with female figurines and pottery in the Olmec style.

lugares/chalcatzingo/resumen.texto: Preclassic site in Morelos with Olmec-style reliefs carved into the rock of the hill, among them “El Rey,” a figure seated inside a cave with rain clouds. It shows the reach of the Olmec style far from the Gulf coast.

lugares/cuicuilco/resumen.texto: Preclassic center in the south of the Valley of Mexico, with a circular pyramid. The eruption of the Xitle volcano, dated by radiocarbon between 245 and 315 although some authors place it before the Common Era, covered it with lava; its decline favored the rise of Teotihuacan.

lugares/izapa/resumen.texto: Center on the Pacific coast of Chiapas whose late Preclassic stelae, with narrative scenes of myths, link Olmec art with Maya art.

lugares/el-mirador/resumen.texto: Large Preclassic Maya city in northern Petén, with the La Danta complex, about 70 meters tall and among the most voluminous buildings of the ancient world, and causeways linking it with Nakbé and other centers. It was abandoned around the 2nd century, in a Preclassic collapse whose causes are debated, and reoccupied on a smaller scale in the Late Classic.

lugares/aguada-fenix/resumen.texto: Artificial platform 1,400 meters long in Tabasco, discovered with lidar in 2017 and published by Takeshi Inomata in 2020: it is the oldest and largest known Maya monumental construction, built around 1000–800 BC and, according to its excavators, showing no signs of a powerful ruler.

lugares/kaminaljuyu/resumen.texto: Major Maya highland center in the Guatemala Valley, at its peak in the Late Preclassic, with Early Classic tombs containing objects in Teotihuacan style. The expansion of Guatemala City destroyed most of the site.

lugares/san-bartolo/resumen.texto: Maya site in northeastern Petén where William Saturno found murals from the 1st century BC and hieroglyphic texts from around 300–200 BC, among the oldest examples of Maya writing.

lugares/san-jose-mogote/resumen.texto: The oldest permanent farming village in the Valley of Oaxaca, with defensive palisades, public buildings and Monument 3, which for Flannery and Marcus is the first example of Zapotec writing. It became subordinate to Monte Albán when the new capital was founded.

lugares/monte-alban/resumen.texto: Zapotec capital founded around 500 BC on the flattened summit of a hill above the Valley of Oaxaca. It has the Danzantes, more than 300 slabs depicting dead or sacrificed enemies, and Building J with conquest slabs, and it dominated the valley until its abandonment between 700 and 850. In Tomb 7, reused by the Mixtecs, Alfonso Caso found a treasure of gold and jade in 1932.

lugares/mitla/resumen.texto: Zapotec religious center of the Postclassic, Lyobaa, with palaces decorated with stone mosaics in fret patterns. 17th-century friars described there the residence of the Zapotec high priest and places of sacrifice; a colonial church was built over part of the complex.

lugares/yagul/resumen.texto: Fortified Zapotec city in the Valley of Oaxaca, at its peak in the Postclassic, with one of the largest ball courts in Mesoamerica. Together with Mitla and the Guilá Naquitz caves, it forms part of the World Heritage site that holds very early evidence of plant domestication.

lugares/cholula/resumen.texto: City in the Puebla Valley inhabited without interruption since the Preclassic, with the Great Pyramid (Tlachihualtepetl), the largest in volume in the world, built in stages between the 3rd century BC and the 9th century. In the Postclassic it was the great sanctuary of Quetzalcoatl and a center of pilgrimage and trade.

lugares/cacaxtla/resumen.texto: Fortified center in Tlaxcala, associated with the Olmeca-Xicalanca, with Epiclassic murals whose colors are very well preserved. The Battle Mural shows jaguar warriors defeating, mutilating and disemboweling warriors dressed as birds and with features in Maya style.

lugares/xochicalco/resumen.texto: Fortified city on a hilltop in Morelos that grew after the fall of Teotihuacan, with the Temple of the Feathered Serpent decorated with reliefs of lords and calendar signs. It was burned and abandoned around 900.

lugares/cantona/resumen.texto: Fortified city in Puebla on a lava flow, which controlled obsidian sources and has more than twenty ball courts, the largest number known at a single site.

lugares/tula/resumen.texto: Toltec capital in Hidalgo, at its peak between 900 and 1150, with stone atlantes depicting warriors, a wall of serpents devouring skeletons, chac mools and a tzompantli, a rack of skulls. It was burned around 1150–1200; the Mexica looted it and idealized it as the Tollan of artists and sages.

lugares/el-tajin/resumen.texto: Large city in central Veracruz, with the Pyramid of the Niches and at least seventeen ball courts. The reliefs of the South Ball Game show the sacrifice of a player by decapitation or heart extraction. The attribution of the city to the Totonacs, who lived in the region in the 16th century, is debated.

lugares/la-quemada/resumen.texto: Fortified city on a hill in Zacatecas, at the northern edge of Mesoamerica, with a hall of columns and causeways. Large quantities of human bones were found in its buildings, including skulls and long bones with cut marks, interpreted as remains of displayed enemies or revered ancestors; it was burned around 900.

lugares/guachimontones/resumen.texto: Center of the Teuchitlán tradition, in Jalisco, with stepped circular pyramids surrounded by platforms, an architecture unique in Mesoamerica. The region had previously been known for its looted shaft tombs.

lugares/tikal/resumen.texto: One of the largest Maya cities, in Petén, capital of a dynasty of about thirty-three kings. After the “entrance” linked with Teotihuacan in 378, it was the great rival of Calakmul: defeated in 562, without monuments for more than a century, it recovered with the victory of 695 and was abandoned in the 10th century.

lugares/uaxactun/resumen.texto: Neighboring city of Tikal, with one of the earliest astronomical complexes of the Group E type. Its monuments record the arrival of Siyaj K'ak' in 378, after which it fell into Tikal's orbit.

lugares/calakmul/resumen.texto: Large Maya city in Campeche, seat since the 7th century of the Snake dynasty (Kaanul), which headed a network of vassal kingdoms against Tikal. It has one of the largest pyramids in the Maya area and more than one hundred stelae, heavily eroded.

lugares/caracol/resumen.texto: Maya city in western Belize whose Altar 21 records the defeat of Tikal in 562, in alliance with Calakmul. A 2009 lidar survey revealed an urban core and agricultural terraces spreading over about 200 square kilometers.

lugares/naranjo/resumen.texto: Maya city in eastern Petén, defeated by Caracol in 631 and refounded in 682 by Lady Six Sky, daughter of the king of Dos Pilas, who ruled it in practice together with her son and through her military campaigns.

lugares/dos-pilas/resumen.texto: Maya city in the Petexbatún region, founded by a branch of the Tikal dynasty, which allied with Calakmul and defeated Tikal in 679. After a defeat in 761, its inhabitants dismantled the palaces to build defensive walls, and the dynasty took refuge in Aguateca.

lugares/aguateca/resumen.texto: Maya city on a cliff in the Petexbatún, protected by walls, the last refuge of the Dos Pilas dynasty. It was attacked and burned around 810 and abandoned suddenly: Takeshi Inomata found the elite houses with their objects still in place.

lugares/cancuen/resumen.texto: Commercial Maya city on the banks of the Pasión River, with one of the largest palaces in the Maya world, a vassal of Calakmul in the 7th century. Around 800 its royal family and nobility were massacred and the city was abandoned.

lugares/bonampak/resumen.texto: Small Maya city in Chiapas, near the Usumacinta and dependent on Yaxchilán, known for the murals of its Structure 1, painted around 790, with a battle, the torture of captives and court rituals.

lugares/yaxchilan/resumen.texto: Maya city on a bend of the Usumacinta, rival of Piedras Negras, with finely carved lintels showing captures of enemies and bloodletting rites. Its peak came under Itzamnaaj B'alam III and his son Yaxun B'alam IV, in the 8th century.

lugares/piedras-negras/resumen.texto: Maya city on the Usumacinta, in Guatemala, whose stelae allowed Tatiana Proskouriakoff to demonstrate in 1960 that the inscriptions recorded the lives of rulers.

lugares/palenque/resumen.texto: Maya city in the Chiapas highlands, capital of the kingdom of B'aakal, with the Palace, the Group of the Crosses and the Temple of the Inscriptions, where Pakal's tomb is. Its texts, among the most extensive of the Classic period, were decisive for decipherment; the city stopped erecting monuments after 799.

lugares/tonina/resumen.texto: Maya city in the valleys of Chiapas, with sculptures of bound, naked captives. In 711 it captured the king of Palenque, K'inich K'an Joy Chitam II; its Monument 101 bears the last known Long Count date, from the year 909.

lugares/copan/resumen.texto: Maya city in western Honduras, capital of a dynasty of sixteen kings founded in 426 by K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo', with high-relief stelae, Altar Q and the Hieroglyphic Stairway. The capture of its king by Quiriguá in 738 weakened its power; it stopped erecting monuments around 822. The valley was occupied long before 426.

lugares/quirigua/resumen.texto: Maya city in the Motagua Valley, in Guatemala, a vassal of Copán until 738, when its king captured and sacrificed the king of Copán. It has the tallest Maya stelae, such as Stela E, more than ten meters high.

lugares/joya-de-ceren/resumen.texto: Maya farming village in El Salvador buried by the ash of the eruption of Loma Caldera around 600. It preserves houses, storerooms, maize fields and everyday objects as they were left, and shows the lives of ordinary people who do not appear in the inscriptions.

lugares/uxmal/resumen.texto: Capital of the Puuc style in northern Yucatán, at its peak between the 9th and 10th centuries, with the Pyramid of the Magician, the Nunnery Quadrangle and the Governor's Palace. Colonial chronicles link it to the Xiu and the League of Mayapán.

lugares/coba/resumen.texto: Large Maya city in northeastern Yucatán, among lagoons, with more than fifty causeways (sacbeob), one of them about one hundred kilometers long to Yaxuná, and the Nohoch Mul pyramid.

lugares/mayapan/resumen.texto: Walled city in Yucatán, the political capital of the northern Maya between the 13th and 15th centuries, with about four thousand structures and an estimated population of more than fifteen thousand. Ruled by the Cocom, it fell around the middle of the 15th century in a rebellion led by the Xiu; excavations found pits with dismembered and burned human remains from that period.

lugares/tulum/resumen.texto: Walled Maya city on a Caribbean cliff, a port for the Postclassic coastal trade. Spaniards of Juan de Grijalva's expedition saw it from the sea in 1518, and compared it to Seville.

lugares/lamanai/resumen.texto: Maya city in northern Belize, inhabited for about three thousand years, without the abandonment that other cities suffered in the Classic collapse. Franciscans built two churches there in the 16th century; the Maya rebelled in 1640 and burned the second.

lugares/qumarkaj/resumen.texto: Capital of the K'iche' kingdom, in the highlands of Guatemala, founded around 1400, which dominated much of the neighboring peoples in the 15th century. In 1524 Pedro de Alvarado burned its rulers alive and set the city on fire; its stones were used to build Santa Cruz del Quiché.

lugares/iximche/resumen.texto: Capital of the Kaqchikel, founded around 1470 after their break with the K'iche'. In 1524 the Kaqchikel received Pedro de Alvarado as allies, and the first Spanish city of Guatemala was founded there; that same year they rebelled over tribute and the city was abandoned.

lugares/zaculeu/resumen.texto: Capital of the Mam in the Guatemalan highlands, surrounded by ravines. In 1525 Gonzalo de Alvarado besieged it for months, and its lord, Kayb'il B'alam, surrendered from hunger.

lugares/mixco-viejo/resumen.texto: Fortified Postclassic city in the Guatemalan highlands, identified as the capital of the Chajoma, conquered by the Spaniards and their allies in 1525 and then abandoned.

lugares/ihuatzio/resumen.texto: Purépecha center on the shore of Lake Pátzcuaro, one of the three seats of the kingdom according to the Relación de Michoacán, with yácatas (pyramids of mixed plan) and walled causeways.

lugares/tzintzuntzan/resumen.texto: Capital of the Purépecha kingdom on the shore of Lake Pátzcuaro, with five yácatas on a large platform. In the 16th century it had, according to archaeological estimates, several tens of thousands of inhabitants; there resided the cazonci, who submitted to the Spaniards in 1522.

lugares/paquime/resumen.texto: Multistory adobe city in northern Chihuahua, center of the Casas Grandes culture, with ball courts, breeding grounds for macaws brought from the south, copper objects and shells from the Gulf of California: the link between Mesoamerica and the peoples of the southwestern United States. Charles Di Peso excavated it between 1958 and 1961; it was burned and abandoned around 1450.
